title: I Lost my Mind: Leave a Legal Move
summary: With two queens, restrict the opposing king without accidentally removing every legal move.

nodes.question: Black has two queens. Which queen move avoids the stalemate trap?
nodes.explanation: White has Kc5 and c4; Black has Kd7, Qf3 and Qe2. White’s pawn is blocked by its own king. Before tightening the cage, count the king’s legal moves.

branches.title: Independent alternative: leave two flights, then mate
commentary: Begin after Kc5 at 12 seconds. The source shows Black throwing away this win with ...Qb2. This winning comparison is independently selected, not a continuation played in the video.
Qb3 leaves White two legal moves, Kd4 and Kd5. The c-pawn remains blocked, but the king is not stalemated.
Kd4 chooses one of those two flights. White still loses with best play; the other king move is checked in a separate branch.
Qbxc4# takes the pawn with the queen from b3, checking the adjacent king. Qe2 protects c4 and covers escape squares, so White cannot capture the checking queen or escape.

branches.title: Independent alternative: the king chooses d5
commentary: This independently selected branch checks the other legal king response to ...Qb3.
Qb3 keeps the win by leaving Kd4 and Kd5 available. It is one winning method, not a uniqueness claim.
Kd5 uses the other flight. White’s pawn is still on c4 and remains a mating target.
Qbxc4# captures with the b3 queen and mates along the c4-d5 diagonal. Qe2 and Qc4 cover the king’s escape squares, and the black king on d7 helps control the sixth rank.

branches.title: Source error: shut every door
commentary: The source illustrates Black moving the e2 queen to b2 in this exact five-piece ending.

Qb2 is stalemate, not mate. White’s king on c5 is not attacked; Qb2, Qf3 and Kd7 cover every available king square, while c4 cannot advance into its own king. White has no legal move and the win becomes a draw.

exercises.prompt: Why is a queen move that leaves an escape square useful here?
exercises.answer: White has no pawn move because Kc5 blocks c4. Leaving Kd4 or Kd5 avoids stalemate and lets Black finish with a protected queen capture.

exercises.prompt: Does having two queens change the stalemate rule?
exercises.answer: No. If White is not in check and has no legal move, the game is drawn regardless of Black’s extra material.
